title: Hire for trajectory, not just résumé
body: How much someone has grown across their last two roles predicts more about their future than their current title does.

title: A players and C players
body: A players hire A players; B players hire C players.
author: Steve Jobs

title: Generalist vs. specialist
body: Final round: a strong generalist who'd need ramp time, versus a deep specialist who has plateaued in past roles. Which matters more?

options.label: Depends whether you are hiring for the next 6 months or the next 3 years — decide that first

explanation: The right answer is entirely dependent on time horizon. Deciding what you are actually hiring for should come before comparing candidates against it.

title: Lowering the bar under pressure
body: A team lowered its hiring bar to hit a headcount target for the quarter. It spent the next eighteen months managing out that hire and rebuilding the team's trust in the process. A bad hire costs far more than an open seat costs in velocity.

title: Name your one non-negotiable
body: Write down, in one sentence, the single non-negotiable trait for your next open role. If you can't name one, you don't have a bar yet.

title: Ask references for a story, not a rating
body: "Tell me about a time they had to deliver bad news" surfaces more than "would you rate them 8 out of 10?" ever will.

title: Design the first 30 days before day one
body: The highest-leverage retention lever is not compensation — it is whether a new hire gets a clear, visible win in their first month.

title: Culture fit vs. culture add
body: An interview panel kept passing on strong candidates for not being a "culture fit" — on inspection, the pattern was that everyone already on the team had the same background. Hiring for culture add, not fit, is what actually raises the bar.

title: Write the scorecard before the first interview
body: Decide what "great" looks like for the role, in writing, before meeting anyone. Otherwise the first strong personality you meet quietly becomes the bar.

title: A rejected candidate is a future referral
body: How you close out a "no" shapes whether that person ever applies again — or recommends someone else who should.

title: The loop that waited for one more signal
body: A hiring loop kept extending because every interviewer wanted "one more signal" before deciding. Six weeks later, the strongest candidate had accepted another offer. Indecision has a cost measured in candidates, not just time.

title: Write your assessment before anyone else speaks
body: Debrief your next interview loop by writing your own assessment before hearing anyone else's. If you always agree with whoever speaks first, you don't have independent signal.

title: Interview for the failure mode, not just the strength
body: Ask what happens when this person is stressed, wrong, or under-resourced. The strength already sold you — the failure mode is what you will actually manage.

title: They remind me of myself
body: An interviewer wants to hire a candidate mainly because they remind the interviewer of themselves early in their career. What is the risk?

options.label: None — similarity is a reasonable predictor of success
Affinity bias — treating "familiar" as a proxy for "qualified"
The candidate is probably overqualified for the role
There is no risk if the candidate also passed the technical bar

explanation: Affinity bias is one of the most common ways a hiring bar quietly erodes. "Reminds me of me" is not a scorecard criterion, however technically strong the candidate also is.

title: A work sample beats a conversation
body: Wherever possible, see the candidate do a scaled-down version of the actual job. It beats any amount of talking about how they would do it.
